title: How much of 'semantic systems are efficient' is the efficiency of a structural constraint? A weighting-free comparison across indefinites, modals and quantifiers

cost.compute_notes: Reuses the re-implementations in denic2022-*/reanalysis/core.py and imel2026-modal-typology-efficiency/reanalysis/mcore.py, and the saved per-language samples in steinertthrelkeld2021-*/reanalysis/out/out_q2_ladder.json. One script, about two minutes. Colour (zaslavsky2018) not included: per-draw complexity/accuracy of the convex null were not saved, and recomputing needs the 73 MB model again.

claims.statement: Measured by net Pareto dominance (P(natural dominates null) - P(null dominates natural), on complexity and informativeness, weighting-free), natural systems overwhelmingly beat random systems of the same size in all three domains (+0.92 indefinites, +0.96 modals, +0.62 quantifiers), and a descriptor-matched structural null removes 84% of that advantage for indefinites, more than all of it for modals, and 41% for quantifiers.
claims.scope: Indefinites: 40 Haspelmath languages vs overlap-free systems with the same size and coverage. Modals: 28 inventories (drop_syn branch) vs distinct IFF systems with the same size, coverage and overlap; Table-5 prior. Quantifiers: no attested inventories; 'natural' = languages drawn from the 101 quasi-natural quantifiers, vs languages of fully monotone and conservative non-natural quantifiers of the same size, complexity NOT matched.

quantities.name: net_pareto_dominance_vs_structural_null
quantities.baseline: indefinites; vs random items of same size +0.923 (0.892-0.948)

quantities.name: net_pareto_dominance_vs_structural_null
quantities.baseline: modals; vs random meanings of same size +0.956 (0.936-0.974)

quantities.name: net_pareto_dominance_vs_structural_null
quantities.baseline: quantifiers; vs random non-natural same size +0.622 (0.593-0.652). With complexity matched per quantifier the sign reverses (steinertthrelkeld2021#c1: d .0435 vs .0486, informativeness favours the structural null)

our_assessment.why: This replaces the 'about nine-tenths in every domain' phrasing I used earlier the same day, which compared gap shares built in different geometries (cidral was asked to attack exactly that). In a common, weighting-free metric the pattern is real but uneven. Indefinites: a small positive residual for natural systems remains (CI excludes 0). Modals: natural systems are WORSE than the structural null. Quantifiers: a large residual remains, and it is entirely formula length -- quasi-natural quantifiers are shorter in the LoT, and when complexity is matched the structural null wins on informativeness. Common thread: wherever natural systems retain an edge over the structural null, the edge is on the COMPLEXITY axis, and complexity is measured in a representation language designed by theorists of the same phenomena (Haspelmath's features; the quantifier LoT; the modal LoT whose atoms are the IFF axes). No domain shows an informativeness advantage over the structural null. Caveat that limits all of this: matching on descriptors such as overlap conditions on something that is itself a route to efficiency, so 'removed by structure' means 'decomposed into', not 'explained away'.

open_questions: Add colour: rerun zaslavsky2018 c2 saving IB complexity and accuracy per Voronoi draw (needs the 73 MB model), then compute the same net dominance.
Which descriptors to match is a choice. Report the full ladder (size -> +distinct -> +coverage -> +overlap) per domain and say where the residual crosses zero, rather than one matched null.

Independent complexity measures (vocabulary size, entropy, a learned LoT) would test whether the remaining complexity-axis edge is a property of languages or of the representation language. imel2026 already shows natural modals lose their edge under vocabulary size and entropy.
